A box-shaped barge 15 m long and 3 m deep. Archimedes' principle gives how deep it floats (mass = water density × length × beam × draught), and its first steadiness comes from the metacentric height GM = KB + BM − KG, with KB = T/2 and BM = B²/(12T). The lean from off-centre cargo uses tan φ = cargo × offset / (mass × GM). The numbers are checked against a sum worked by hand. It is only right for small leans while the deck stays dry. It leaves out waves, wind, the curved shape of real hulls, liquids sloshing in tanks and cargo that slides; the rocking you see is the steady lean a 30 t·m sideways push would give, applied to and fro.

A globe tilted by 23.44° circling the Sun once in 365 days. The Sun's declination is −tilt × cos(2π(N + 10) / 365) for day N, the length of the day comes from cos ω = −tan(latitude) × tan(declination) with the Sun up or down all day near the poles, and the noon Sun stands 90° − |latitude − declination| above the horizon. It is checked against four known results: 12 hours at the equator all year, 12 hours everywhere at an equinox, 24 hours at 66.56° north on the June solstice, and an overhead noon Sun on the Tropic of Cancer that day. It leaves out the bending of light by the air and the width of the Sun's disc (together they add a few minutes of daylight), the slightly uneven speed of the Earth along its orbit, leap years, mountains and time zones. The lamp, globe and orbit are not drawn to scale.

A motor that holds 600 rpm and can give up to 2.4 N·m drives a rope drum (radius 0.05 m) through two pairs of gears. For each pair, gear ratio = driven teeth ÷ driver teeth; torque is multiplied by the ratio and by the efficiency, speed is divided by the ratio, and power in = power out ÷ efficiency. It is checked against known results: 20 → 60 teeth gives three times the torque at a third of the speed, and power is conserved at 100 % efficiency. It leaves out the weight and stretch of the rope, the time the motor needs to speed up, tooth strength and wear, and the way a real motor slows down under load: here it either holds its speed or cannot turn at all.

A simplified picture of the mouth, not a full model of a voice. The first two resonances (formants F1 and F2) are found by a straight-line blend between typical adult values for the corner vowels: i about 280 / 2250 Hz, a about 750 / 1300 Hz and u about 310 / 870 Hz. A higher tongue lowers F1, a tongue further forward raises F2, and rounding the lips lowers F2. Real voices differ: children and smaller speakers have higher formants, every language and accent places its vowels a little differently, and real formants do not change in straight lines. It leaves out the third and higher resonances, the nose, the pitch and loudness of the voice, and all consonants. The Listen sound is a plain buzz passed through two filters, not a recording of a person.

A strong acid (hydrochloric acid, HCl) mixed with a strong base (sodium hydroxide, NaOH) at 25 °C. Both are treated as fully split into ions, the volumes simply add, and the pH comes from the exact charge balance with water's own ions included (Kw = 1.0 × 10⁻¹⁴), so it is correct right at neutral. Checked against textbook values: pH 1.00 at the start, 7.00 at the equivalence point and 11.96 with 5 mL too much base. It leaves out activity effects in strong solutions, carbon dioxide from the air, temperature changes from the heat of the reaction, and the small errors of a real burette and a real indicator.

A textbook market with two straight lines. Shoppers want 100 loaves minus 10 for every token of price (130 on a festival day). Bakers bring 10 loaves plus 5 for every token they keep after tax. The lines cross at price = (a − c + d × tax) ÷ (b + d), and a tax is shared in the ratio b : d. These answers are exact for this model and are checked by hand-worked sums. Real markets are not straight lines and people are not identical: some shoppers love bread and some do not, bakers have different ovens and costs, prices change slowly, and people also think about quality, habit and fairness. Money here is the game's pretend tokens.

An exact count of ranked ballots under three rules: most first choices; instant run-off (while no project has more than half, the one with the fewest ballots drops out and its ballots pass to their next choice); and points (3 for a first choice, 2 for a second, 1 for a third). It also works out which project would beat each other one head-to-head. The counts are checked against two ballot sets worked out by hand (21 ballots and 25 ballots) where the three rules choose three different winners. It leaves out ties (the ballot sets are chosen so that none happen), ballots that rank only some projects, people who vote cleverly instead of honestly, people who do not vote, and the many other counting rules that exist.

An ideal string held at both ends: the wave speed is √(tension ÷ mass per metre) and the n-th standing wave has the frequency (n ÷ 2L) × wave speed. Notes are named in equal temperament with A4 = 440 Hz, and 100 cents is one piano key. The tension comes from a hanging weight (tension = mass × 9.81 m/s²). The picture is slowed down several hundred times and the swing is drawn much bigger than life. It leaves out the stiffness of the string, air drag and the way a real string fades, the small stretch that raises the tension when you pluck hard, and the mix of many harmonics that gives each instrument its own sound.

Cardiac output = heart rate × stroke volume (70 beats a minute × 70 mL = 4.9 litres a minute). Oxygen delivered = cardiac output × the oxygen the body takes from each litre of blood. It uses typical textbook adult values: about 50 mL of oxygen per litre at rest, 80 when walking and 140 when running; needs of about 250, 800 and 2,400 mL a minute; and a highest heart rate of roughly 220 minus age (190 for a 30-year-old), which is only a rough guide. Real bodies vary a lot and adjust many things at once: breathing, blood vessels, blood pressure and how the blood is shared out, none of which are shown here. It is for learning how the heart works, not for judging anyone's health.

Each round is an exact random experiment: the lantern is equally likely to be behind any door, you pick a door at random, the guide (who knows where the lantern is) opens every other door but one and never opens the lantern's door, and then you stick or switch. Counting every case gives exactly 1 in 3 for sticking and 2 in 3 for switching, or (N − 1) in N with N doors; a seeded run of 30,000 rounds is checked against those values. It leaves out a guide who opens doors without knowing, a guide who only sometimes offers the switch, and any clue such as light under a door.

Every ball meets one peg in each row and goes right with the chance you choose, otherwise left; every choice is independent of the ones before it. The number of rights decides the bin, so the piles follow the binomial distribution: the chance of bin k is (number of paths to k) × p^k × (1 − p)^(rows − k). The model is checked against that formula: the chances add up to 1, 10 rows at 50% peak in bin 5 with 252/1024, and 20,000 drops match every bin within 3 standard errors. It leaves out everything a real board adds: balls bumping into each other and the walls, spin, friction and pegs that are not perfectly even. The hops you see are a drawing of each ball's path, not a physics calculation.

Exact logic, not an estimate: a queen sees every square along its row, its column and both diagonals, and two queens are in conflict when one stands on a square the other sees. The number of solutions is counted by a backtracking search and matches the known results (2, 10, 4, 40 and 92 for boards of 4 to 8 squares a side). It leaves out every other chess piece, taking turns and capturing, and it counts turned-round and mirrored arrangements as different solutions.

Radioactive decay of carbon-14 with a half-life of 5,730 years: the share that is left equals one half raised to the power (age ÷ 5,730). The model is checked at one, two and three half-lives. It ignores calibration curves (the amount of carbon-14 in the air has changed a little over time, so real laboratories correct their dates against tree rings) and contamination by newer or older carbon, and the meter here reads the exact share with no measuring error. The method only works for things that were once alive, and only back to roughly 50,000 years.

Reading = 400 µSv/h × e^(−μx) × (1 m ÷ d)² × (½)^(t ÷ 6 h): exponential attenuation in a flat shield of thickness x, the inverse-square law for distance d, and radioactive decay over time t. The attenuation coefficients are for gamma rays of about 1 MeV: water 0.0707, concrete 0.147, steel 0.472 and lead 0.806 per cm. The detector gives 5 counts each second for every µSv/h, with natural counting scatter. It is checked against three known results: one half-value layer (ln 2 ÷ μ) halves the reading, twice the distance quarters it, and one half-life halves it. It leaves out scattered rays that build up behind thick shields, natural background radiation, the size of the source and the air in between. The source is a practice one with a 6-hour half-life, not a particular real isotope.

The classic five-part plot shape: beginning (exposition), rising action, climax, falling action and resolution. Each scene lists what a reader must already know, and the order is accepted only when nothing happens before its cause. Tension is a simple score from 0 to 10 for each scene, and the line must rise to a single peak at the climax and then fall. This is one useful pattern among many, not a rule. Many great stories and many cultures' tales are shaped differently: some begin in the middle, some go round in a circle, some are a chain of episodes, and some have no single peak at all. The model leaves out character, language, theme, humour and everything else that makes a story worth reading.

Two idealised models. Light (additive): the red, green and blue lamps are added together in each channel, so red + green = yellow and all three = white. Paint (subtractive): each pigment removes only its opposite colour from white paper (red = 1 − cyan, green = 1 − magenta, blue = 1 − yellow), so cyan + yellow = green and all three = black. Distance is the straight-line gap between two colours, 0 % to 100 %. Real paints and screens are less pure than this: real pigments soak up some of every colour, so mixed paint looks duller and all three make a muddy brown, and real lamps and screens cannot show every colour the eye can see. It also leaves out how the eye judges brightness.
